methodology: Ranks the 46 U.S. states not yet covered by GridPermit (CA, RI, DE, VT already have at least one record — see docs/DATA_ARCHITECTURE.md) by expected ease of reaching genuine, honestly-sourced READY coverage. Two source tiers are mixed here and explicitly labeled per-state in `notes`: (1) DIRECTLY SOURCED this session from DSIRE (programs.dsireusa.org, filtered to Program Type = 'Solar/Wind Permitting Standards') and the SolarAPP+ Foundation's own jurisdiction table (gosolarapp.org/where-is-solarapp-available), including a corroborated finding that Colorado's DORA issues a single statewide electrical permit for residential solar covering 200+ Colorado jurisdictions (dpo.colorado.gov/ElectricalPlumbingPermits, gosolarapp.org/landing-pages/solarapp-colorado); (2) GENERAL STRUCTURAL/CIVICS KNOWLEDGE not independently re-verified this session — county/municipality counts and which utility dominates which state are treated as low-risk public-record facts, not case-by-case regulatory claims, but were not re-confirmed against a primary source for every state the way DSIRE/SolarAPP+ was. No locality-level research was performed for any of these 46 states — this file is a prioritization map only, not a data-collection input.

states.name: Colorado
states.permitting_model: mixed — building permit is municipal/county, but electrical permit for residential solar is issued statewide by one agency
states.approx_meaningful_ahjs: ~64 counties + ~270 municipalities for the building-permit side, but effectively 1 for the electrical-permit side
states.utility_concentration: high — Xcel Energy (Public Service Co. of Colorado) dominates the Front Range/Denver metro population majority; rural co-ops elsewhere
states.city_by_city_research_likely: low for electrical permitting (one statewide fact covers 200+ jurisdictions); still needed for building-permit authority/fees per city
states.confidence: high — directly sourced via DORA's own site (dpo.colorado.gov), SolarAPP+'s own jurisdiction table, and DSIRE's 'Solar Construction Permitting Standards' (CO) entry
states.notes: Standout finding: Colorado's Department of Regulatory Agencies (DORA) issues a single 'Colorado State Electrical (Photovoltaic)' permit valid statewide, and per SolarAPP+'s own announcement this covers electrical plan review for 200+ Colorado jurisdictions. This is a single, massively reusable state-level fact — likely the highest-leverage finding of this whole priority pass.

states.name: Arizona
states.permitting_model: municipal/county — mostly city building departments; county for unincorporated areas
states.approx_meaningful_ahjs: 15 counties + ~91 incorporated municipalities — low for a state this size
states.utility_concentration: high — APS, SRP, and TEP together cover the large majority of the state's population
states.utility_data_accessibility: likely good — large Sun Belt solar market, well-documented utilities
states.city_by_city_research_likely: yes, but low AHJ count keeps the total burden manageable
states.confidence: high on the statewide-rule/utility-concentration facts (DSIRE-sourced); AHJ count and code coverage are structural/general knowledge, not re-verified
states.notes: DSIRE lists a dedicated 'Solar Construction Permitting Standards' (AZ) entry plus a Maricopa Association of Governments regional standard — signals a mature, coordinated statewide solar-permitting practice, similar in spirit to California's AB 2188.

states.name: Hawaii
states.permitting_model: county — Hawaii is the only U.S. state with zero incorporated municipalities; each of its 4 counties (Honolulu, Maui, Hawaii, Kauai) is the sole building-permit authority for its entire land area
states.approx_meaningful_ahjs: 4 — the lowest of any state by a wide margin
states.utility_concentration: high — Hawaiian Electric (HECO) serves Oahu, Maui, and Hawaii Island; Kauai Island Utility Cooperative (KIUC) serves Kauai
states.municipal_code_coverage_strength: not applicable — no municipal code layer exists
states.city_by_city_research_likely: no — county-by-county only, and there are only 4
states.confidence: high on the '4 counties, no municipalities' structural fact (well-established, not independently re-verified this session but very low-risk); no DSIRE statewide-permitting-law entry was found in this session's scan, and utility/code data accessibility was not checked
states.notes: Very low ceiling (a maximum of 4 possible locality records, ever) but each one is reachable with no city-by-city research at all — the fastest possible full-state completion, not the highest-volume one. Hawaii also has the highest per-capita residential solar adoption in the U.S., suggesting official material likely exists, but this was not confirmed this session.

states.name: Oregon
states.permitting_model: municipal/county — mostly city building departments; county for unincorporated areas
states.utility_concentration: high — Portland General Electric and PacifiCorp (Pacific Power) together cover the large majority of the state's population, alongside several municipal utilities (e.g. Eugene Water & Electric Board)
states.confidence: high on the statewide-rule fact (DSIRE-sourced, plus a separate 'City of Portland - Streamlined Building Permits for Residential Solar Systems' entry and a statewide model ordinance); utility/AHJ-count figures are structural/general knowledge
states.notes: DSIRE lists both a statewide 'Solar Permitting Law' and a Portland-specific streamlined-permit policy — two separate, corroborating signals of a mature statewide solar-permitting practice.

states.name: New Mexico
states.permitting_model: municipal/county — mostly city building departments; county for unincorporated areas
states.utility_concentration: high — Public Service Company of New Mexico (PNM) dominates the majority of the state's population
states.confidence: high on the statewide-rule fact (DSIRE 'Solar/Wind Construction Permitting Standards' entry); utility/AHJ-count figures are structural/general knowledge
states.notes: One of only 6 states this session found a dedicated, statewide (not just county/city model-ordinance) DSIRE 'Solar/Wind Permitting Standards' entry for, alongside CA, IL, NJ, OR, and CO.

states.name: Nevada
states.permitting_model: municipal/county — mostly city building departments; county for unincorporated areas
states.approx_meaningful_ahjs: 17 counties + ~19 incorporated cities — very low for a state this size
states.utility_concentration: very high — NV Energy is a near-monopoly across the large majority of the state
states.city_by_city_research_likely: yes, but the AHJ count is very low
states.confidence: moderate — no DSIRE statewide solar-permitting-law entry was found this session for NV, so this score rests mainly on the low AHJ count and utility concentration, both structural/general knowledge, not re-verified
states.notes: No dedicated statewide permitting-standards DSIRE entry found this session — unlike CO/AZ/OR/NM/IL/NJ, Nevada's ease here is driven by structure (few AHJs, one dominant utility), not a confirmed state law.

states.name: Illinois
states.permitting_model: municipal/county — mostly city building departments; county for unincorporated areas
states.approx_meaningful_ahjs: ~1,300 municipalities — high fragmentation, offsetting the statewide rule's benefit
states.utility_concentration: high — ComEd (Chicago metro/northern IL) and Ameren Illinois (central/southern IL) together cover nearly the entire state
states.municipal_code_coverage_strength: likely strong for the Chicago metro; not individually verified statewide
states.city_by_city_research_likely: yes, and the sheer number of municipalities is a real drag on throughput despite the statewide rule
states.confidence: high on the statewide-rule fact (DSIRE 'Statewide Renewable Energy Permitting Standards' entry); municipality count is structural/general knowledge
states.notes: Has a genuine statewide permitting standard, but Illinois' ~1,300 municipalities (one of the highest counts of any state) mean the CA-style 'research the state law once, then verify per city quickly' pattern will still involve a very large number of individual city touches to reach broad coverage.

states.name: New Jersey
states.permitting_model: municipal — New Jersey has the strongest 'home rule' tradition in the country; essentially every one of its ~565 municipalities is its own AHJ
states.approx_meaningful_ahjs: ~565 municipalities — very high density of small AHJs for the state's size
states.utility_concentration: moderate-high — PSE&G covers the largest share of the state's population, with JCP&L, Atlantic City Electric, and Orange & Rockland covering the rest
states.city_by_city_research_likely: yes, and municipal fragmentation is a real drag despite the statewide law
states.confidence: high on the statewide-rule fact (DSIRE 'Solar and Wind Permitting Laws' entry, statewide not county/city-scoped); municipality/utility figures are structural/general knowledge
states.notes: Same pattern as Illinois: a confirmed statewide law offset by extreme municipal fragmentation (NJ's home-rule tradition is unusually strong even by East Coast standards).

states.name: Utah
states.permitting_model: municipal/county — mostly city building departments; county for unincorporated areas
states.utility_concentration: high — Rocky Mountain Power (PacifiCorp) dominates the large majority of the state
states.confidence: moderate — no DSIRE statewide solar-permitting-law entry found this session for UT; score driven by utility concentration, structural/general knowledge
states.notes: No confirmed statewide permitting standard found this session.

states.name: Maryland
states.permitting_model: county-leaning — Maryland's 23 counties plus Baltimore City handle most residential building permitting directly, with fewer independent municipal building departments than most East Coast states
states.approx_meaningful_ahjs: 23 counties + Baltimore City — relatively low for the region
states.utility_concentration: moderate — Pepco, BGE (Exelon), Delmarva Power, and Potomac Edison split the state
states.city_by_city_research_likely: lower than most East Coast states — county-based permitting reduces the number of distinct AHJs to research
states.confidence: moderate — the DSIRE entry found ('Permits and Variances for Solar Panels, Calculation of Impervious Cover') is narrower than a full permitting-standards law; AHJ-count/utility figures are structural/general knowledge
states.notes: Maryland's relatively county-centric local-government structure (vs. NJ/PA/NY's dense municipal layers) is the main driver of this score, not a confirmed comprehensive statewide solar-permitting law.

next_tier_not_selected_for_tonight.reason: Seattle-specific DSIRE entry only, not statewide; moderate AHJ count; several utilities including multiple public utility districts.
No statewide solar-permitting DSIRE entry found; independent-city-plus-county structure is a genuine complexity unique to Virginia; Dominion Energy dominant.
DSIRE entries are model/as-of-right ordinances, not a mandatory statewide standard; ~351 cities/towns; Eversource and National Grid cover most of the state.

DSIRE entries found for NC are almost entirely wind-specific county ordinances, not a solar-permitting standard; Duke Energy is highly dominant, a real plus, but county-by-county research still likely required.
Connecticut has no county government at all — all 169 towns are independent AHJs; DSIRE entry found is a local-option fee waiver, not a mandatory statewide standard.
